title: DTFT and Frequency Response
description: Ten original questions on the DTFT, periodicity, transform properties, frequency response, phase delay and moving-average filters. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero. Includes a rational-transform output calculation and a four-tap moving-average response.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the discrete-time Fourier transform $X(e^{j \omega})$ are correct?

options.content: It is periodic in $\omega$ with period $2\pi$.
It is formed by summing $x[n]e^{-j \omega n}$ over integer $n$.
Values outside one period are unrelated to values inside it.
Its frequency variable is continuous even though time is discrete.

questions.explanation: The DTFT maps an integer-indexed sequence to a continuous, $2\pi$-periodic frequency function. Adding $2\pi$ to $\omega$ leaves every exponential basis term unchanged.

questions.prompt: If $x[n]$ has DTFT $X(e^{j \omega})$, what is the DTFT of $x[n-n_0]$?

options.content: $X(e^{j(\omega-n_0)})$
$n_0 X(e^{j \omega})$
$e^{-j \omega n_0}X(e^{j \omega})$
$X(e^{j \omega})$ for every $n_0$

questions.explanation: A delay in time multiplies the spectrum by a linear-phase factor. Its magnitude is one, so the shift changes phase but not the magnitude spectrum.

questions.prompt: For $y[n]=x[n]*h[n]$, which frequency-domain statements are correct?

options.content: Where the transforms are nonzero, output phase is input phase plus system phase modulo $2\pi$.
Linear convolution in time becomes addition in frequency.
$Y(e^{j \omega})=X(e^{j \omega})H(e^{j \omega})$.

questions.explanation: The convolution theorem turns time-domain convolution into frequency-domain multiplication. Magnitudes multiply and phases add, which makes the frequency response a direct description of how an LTI system modifies each frequency.

questions.prompt: If $x[n]$ is real-valued, which symmetries hold for its DTFT?

options.content: The magnitude spectrum is even in frequency.
The phase is odd where a consistent phase representation is defined.
The DTFT must be purely real at every frequency.
$X(e^{-j \omega})$ is the complex conjugate of $X(e^{j \omega})$.

questions.explanation: A real sequence has conjugate-symmetric spectrum. This makes magnitude even and phase odd up to phase wrapping and zeros. The spectrum can still be complex away from special frequencies.

questions.prompt: A zero-state LTI system has $h[n]=3(1/2)^nu[n]$ and input $x[n]=(-1/4)^nu[n]$. Which expression is its output?
questions.explanation: Let $z=e^{-j\omega}$. Then $Y=3/[(1-z/2)(1+z/4)]=2/(1-z/2)+1/(1+z/4)$. Inverting gives the stated output. Independently, y[0]=3 and y[1]=3(-1/4)+3/2=3/4, which reject the distractors. Pointwise multiplication is not LTI convolution.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 6-9 and 15-16; EE3731C ClassicalSignal2Questions.pdf, page 1, Q1

questions.prompt: Because the DTFT is $2\pi$-periodic, its inverse may use the same $1/(2\pi)$ normalization but integrate over any interval of length $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The inverse formula uses a complete $2\pi$ interval: $x[n]=(1/(2\pi))\int_{a}^{a+2\pi}X(e^{j\omega})e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega$. A half-period with the same normalization does not generally recover the sequence. For example, X=1 would give x[0]=1/2 rather than 1.

questions.prompt: A two-sided complex exponential $x[n]=e^{j\omega_0n}$ is applied to an LTI system whose frequency response exists at $\omega_0$. Assume zero-state response. What follows?

options.content: If $H(e^{j\omega_0})\ne0$, the nonzero output has the same frequency $\omega_0$ (modulo $2\pi$).
Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems.
A linear time-invariant system must create unrelated new frequencies from this input.
The complex amplitude is multiplied by $H(e^{j \omega_0})$.

questions.explanation: The output is $y[n]=H(e^{j\omega_0})e^{j\omega_0n}$. A nonzero response scales and phase-shifts the exponential without changing its frequency. If $H(e^{j\omega_0})=0$, the output is the zero sequence; it is then misleading to assign it a unique nonzero oscillation frequency. Zero is an allowed eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has an absolutely summable impulse response. Which statements follow?

options.content: The system is BIBO stable.
Absolute summability alone proves the system is causal.
$|H(e^{j \omega})|$ is bounded by the absolute sum of $h[n]$.
Its frequency response exists as a bounded continuous function.

questions.explanation: Absolute summability is the LTI BIBO-stability condition and guarantees convergence and boundedness of the DTFT. Causality is separate and requires $h[n]=0$ for negative $n$.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 31-34; EE3731C ClassicalSignal2Questions.pdf, page 1, Q4

questions.prompt: A causal moving-average filter has $h[n]=1/4$ for n=0,1,2,3 and zero elsewhere. Which statements are correct?

options.content: Its generalized linear-phase delay is 1.5 samples.
It has unit magnitude at every frequency.
Averaging eliminates a constant input.
Its group delay is four samples everywhere its response is nonzero.

questions.explanation: The response is $H=(1+e^{-j\omega}+e^{-j2\omega}+e^{-j3\omega})/4=e^{-j3\omega/2}\sin(2\omega)/(4\sin(\omega/2))$, using limits at removable singularities. The four coefficients sum to one, while at π/2 their phasors cancel. Symmetry about 1.5 gives that delay away from response zeros; the filter is not all-pass.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 20-21; EE3731C ClassicalSignal2Questions.pdf, page 1, Q2

questions.prompt: Why is a linear phase response often desirable in a filter passband?

options.content: Linear phase always means zero delay.
Frequency components experience a common time delay.
The waveform shape is preserved when magnitude distortion is also controlled.
The phase has the form $-\omega D$ plus a constant over the relevant band.

questions.explanation: A phase proportional to frequency corresponds to a time shift $D$. Equal delay across frequency avoids phase distortion, though the delay need not be zero and the magnitude response can still alter amplitudes.
